subject: Biology
title: Overfishing: Emptying the Sea
description: A 60-second lesson on Overfishing: Emptying the Sea.

hook.text: In 1992, Atlantic cod stocks collapsed after centuries of fishing. 40,000 people lost their jobs overnight.

buildup.text: Industrial fishing fleets use sonar, GPS, and mile-long nets to harvest fish at unsustainable rates.

discovery.text: Over 34% of global fish stocks are now overfished. Another 60% are fished at maximum capacity.

twist.text: Bycatch—unwanted species caught accidentally—kills millions of sharks, turtles, and dolphins each year.

climax.text: Marine protected areas where fishing is banned allow stocks to recover dramatically within a decade.

punchline.text: The ocean feeds a billion people. But not if we empty it first.

quiz.question: What percentage of global fish stocks are overfished?

details.summary: Overfishing has depleted 90 percent of large ocean predators and pushed one-third of commercial fish stocks beyond sustainable limits. Industrial fishing with enormous trawls and long lines extracts fish faster than populations can reproduce, threatening marine food webs.
details.whyItMatters: Overfishing threatens the food security of over 3 billion people who depend on seafood for protein. Collapsing fish stocks devastate fishing economies and cascade through marine ecosystems that depend on balanced predator-prey relationships.
takeaways: About one-third of commercial fish stocks are overfished globally
Industrial fishing has removed an estimated 90 percent of large predatory fish
Bycatch kills millions of non-target animals including dolphins and sea turtles

faq.question: Can overfished stocks recover?
faq.answer: Yes, if given sufficient protection. The North Atlantic swordfish recovered after catch limits were imposed. However, recovery can take decades and requires sustained management. Some collapsed stocks like Atlantic cod have shown painfully slow recovery over 30 years.

faq.question: What is the most sustainable way to eat fish?
faq.answer: Choose species certified by organizations like the Marine Stewardship Council. Favor small, fast-reproducing species like sardines and anchovies over large slow-reproducing predators. Farmed shellfish like mussels and oysters have the lowest environmental impact.
